# Golden Rules for Agentic Engineering

Author: Indrajeet Patil
Format: Quarto RevealJS presentation
Canonical URL: https://www.indrapatil.com/agentic-engineering-golden-rules/
Source: https://github.com/IndrajeetPatil/agentic-engineering-golden-rules/
License: CC0 1.0 Universal
Publication date: 2026-10-08
Language: English

## Summary

This slide deck presents ten golden rules for agentic engineering: using coding agents to boost productivity without compromising quality. Quality depends on the engineering system around the agent: a codebase that is easy to navigate, a deterministic harness that gives fast feedback, observable acceptance criteria, prepared codebase patterns, clean context, useful tools, current prompts and repository guidance as models change, repeatable automation, end-to-end flow improvements, and a team culture that keeps humans responsible for what ships.

The talk is aimed at software engineers who ship production software and have at least some experience with coding agents such as Claude Code or GitHub Copilot CLI.

## The agentic stack

A single tabbed slide introduces the same responsibility diagram for Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub Copilot. An LLM reasons and requests tools; the harness manages context, session state, permissions, and tool execution. The agent is the model and harness working in a task loop. Tool-calling sends an action request and returns its result. A desktop app is the user interface, and model access is a separate service. Examples: Claude Desktop Code tab / Claude Code harness / Claude / Anthropic; ChatGPT desktop Codex workspace / Codex harness / GPT / OpenAI; VS Code Copilot interface / Copilot harness / selected Claude model / Anthropic as model developer, with access through GitHub Copilot. Selecting Claude within Copilot does not select the Claude Code harness. The diagrams show responsibilities, not deployment boundaries.

## The golden rules
1. Prepare the codebase for agents. Agents tend to reproduce patterns the repository exposes, including uneven or suboptimal ones. Pay down high-impact technical debt, make sound conventions easy to find, and establish reliable checks before scaling agent work; this helps prevent existing problems from being repeated in new changes.
2. Improve developer experience. If humans hunt for context, agents burn tokens too. Clear structure, one-command workflows (such as make setup and make qa), deterministic QA, living documentation (including a short AGENTS.md), and modular design help humans and agents alike.
3. Set deterministic quality gates. Let deterministic checks catch what they can, fast. Use formatters, linters, type checkers, and tests to catch repeatable classes of mistakes. A Ruff F841 example shows an unused local variable inside a function, the agent fixing it, and the passing change moving to human review. Checks provide evidence; people still judge whether the work meets the requirements. Never weaken a check merely to get green; repairing an inappropriate gate is deliberate, reviewed work.
4. Define done before delegating. Combine intent with observable acceptance criteria: state the outcome, constraints, what must stay unchanged, and the evidence needed to accept the result. Prescribe steps when sequence matters, such as migrations, incident response, or proven diagnostics. Reproduce bugs before fixing them, inspect rendered UI interactions, and measure performance under comparable conditions. Implementation and tests can share a misunderstanding; compare both with the requirements. Agents verify their own work, inspect results, fix failures, and re-check before handing over evidence for human review.
5. Maintain session hygiene. Coherent context beats haunted context. Long sessions accumulate stale assumptions and conflicting instructions. Default to one task per session, but keep a closely related follow-up in the same session when its reasoning and discoveries still help; restarting can lose a constraint or a failed hypothesis. Length matters as well as coherence, because recall degrades as context grows (context rot); clear context between unrelated tasks and compact only when continuing related work. Use one Git worktree per parallel task so each task has its own working directory, and keep durable conventions, decisions, and lessons in the repository (for example, AGENTS.md) rather than in chat history. Reset with a compact handoff: goal, constraints, relevant files, approaches already ruled out, and acceptance checks.
6. Know thy tools. Sometimes the unlock is a hidden tool affordance. Example affordances that users miss include Claude Code voice dictation, Codex built-in image generation, and GitHub Copilot CLI computer use. Read the changelog; these examples are not exhaustive. Official docs were checked on 8 October 2026. When results are poor, check whether the agent had the right context, tools, and feedback.
7. Keep pace with changing models. Model behaviour and availability can change, so review the whole working system when a model changes: source code, tests, documentation, prompts, and repository guidance such as AGENTS.md. Update only what the change calls for, verify it, and record durable advice in the repository. Anthropic recommends checking model lifecycle updates and testing newer models before retirement.
8. Automate repeated agent work. Capture effective recurring workflows in prompts, skills, slash commands, and multi-step workflows. Choose the smallest reusable mechanism that fits the work; automate coordination while people own evaluation and trade-offs. People set the explicit risk policy for any automatic merge and retain human review for ambiguous, risky, or exceptional changes.
9. Identify and remove bottlenecks. Apply Amdahl’s law as an analogy across the SDLC: accelerating implementation alone cannot remove time spent waiting for review, verification, or release. Locate the current queue, choose a targeted intervention, and measure the full flow again because the constraint can move. Examples include Rust-based tools for slow lint and type checks, splitting or stacking large PRs before an LLM reviewer loop, and task-specific end-to-end tests for slow behaviour checks. The reviewer loop adds capacity; it does not replace human judgement.
10. Be curious. Be humble. Be kind. DHH’s “It’s more fun to be competent” line encourages engineers to keep understanding their systems and building their skills as tools change.

## A low-touch software factory example

The software-factory example uses the public [chatbot-template](https://github.com/IndrajeetPatil/chatbot-template/). Its local `make qa` and `make hooks` commands check changes before a pull request. GitHub Actions runs formatting, linting, type checks, backend and frontend tests, end-to-end browser tests, security checks, and other quality gates. The main-branch ruleset requires `prek`, `test`, `backend`, `frontend`, `e2e`, and `qa` status checks. Frontend pull requests include screenshots under the repository's agent instructions. Those instructions also require a current-head Codex thumbs-up, resolution of review findings, and successful required checks before the coding agent squash-merges. Codex review is an agent-workflow requirement; it is not one of the GitHub ruleset's required statuses. The software-factory illustration shows example gates including full code and type coverage, benchmarks, zero lint issues and warnings, Lighthouse performance, accessibility, and SEO. These are example thresholds, not proof that a change is correct. The team that owns the repository defines which small, reversible changes can auto-merge after all required checks pass. People own that policy, monitor its results, and review changes with higher impact or uncertainty. Agent work is sandboxed with restricted network access and scoped credentials, while repository files and issue text are treated as untrusted input that may contain malicious instructions.

## Conclusion

Good agentic engineering practices can speed up routine work through Plan, Code, Review, Verify, and Release, while quality gates protect standards. People set direction, own risk boundaries, and apply judgement to high-stakes decisions and exceptions.
